items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: The other things were pretty — there were some Paul Whiteman records and stuff like that.

ctx.x: Well Austria, which is where I started out, what I heard of jazz was pretty much limited, as I can tell in retrospect, from records. I liked to — my mother had a wind-up phonograph and I liked to play around with that and also her mother, my mother was one of four siblings, she was the oldest but she had two sisters and the brother. And my grandmother had a place in Upper Bavaria. It was near the Austrian border. But she had

bought that in 1912 to raise her family. I spent my summers there as a kid. And there were a bunch of records that belonged to my mother and her siblings, and there was dance music. But it really turns out in retrospect to have been the closest thing to real jazz was by a British trumpet player named Nat Gonella. He was an Armstrong acolyte when Louis first came to Europe — he came to England in 1932 — Nat was one of the first to welcome him and took him under his wing and got him settled in London and all that.…
You were about nine years old?

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: My first encounter, in retrospect, with anything resembling jazz was when Jack Hylton, the famous English bandleader who had something to do with the careers of Coleman Hawkins and Louis Armstrong, and I think he intersected with Benny Carter as well – anyway, he was like the British Paul Whiteman.

ctx.x: the Nazis were taking over all these bureaucratic positions and didn’t know anything, so she managed to talk them into giving her a Danish passport. The Danish consulate was cooperative, I guess. She dumped me at my grandmother’s place and went to Denmark and prepared things there. Then my grandmother, who was a Danish national by marriage and was free to travel – this is still ’38. Things are not as they became later with closed borders. So we were able to get in Denmark. That was the last time that I saw my…

Anyway, Berg gave me this thing. I really liked it. Then two months later exactly, almost to the day, he was dead. My parents were very upset about this. So I remember that as my first experience with someone close having died. In Vienna my parents – they used to have these things like they have in most civilized times – they have concerts for young kids. So I would be taken to symphony concerts on a Sunday at noon or something like that. I remember I didn’t like the conductor. He was heavy-set, his tuxedo didn’t…

was saying or what he was singing about, except a few words, but he had a lot of movement. It was something that made an impression on me. My mother liked him a lot too. What she liked best was one thing that he did in that show. One of the songs – was it – that he called Believe it Beloved. That was on a record. We bought that. That was my first Fats Waller record. I had, as I said earlier, liked the phonographs. I wasn’t really collecting records, but as a kid – I can pretty well tell you what I started…
